did_you_know.text: In the Bible, “hearing the voice of an oath” means hearing a formal oath or curse. A person who knows the truth but stays silent is held responsible for that silence.
This verse teaches that words spoken in an oath create a real obligation, whether a person swears to do something good or to refrain from doing it.
The rules of the offering take a person’s financial situation into account: someone who cannot afford a sheep may bring two birds instead.
Even a tenth of an ephah of fine flour can serve as a sin offering for the poorest person. Unlike an ordinary grain offering, it is brought without oil or frankincense.
The “sacred shekel” was an official standard of weight used in Temple matters; it does not necessarily refer to a particular coin.
The extra fifth that the guilty person must add is one-fifth of the original amount—an additional twenty percent.
Here, a guilt offering is required even when a person does not know which commandment was violated. The Torah thus emphasizes that ignorance does not completely remove responsibility.
The list includes mishandling a deposit, robbery, oppression, and denying property entrusted to someone. It highlights how important trust between people is to society.
Repair begins with returning the property to its owner, and only afterward is the guilt offering brought. The Torah teaches that a religious ritual cannot replace repairing harm done to others.
